Ultimate 1-50: the male footballers best associated with each squad number

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5460 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theguardian

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, who is football’s most legendary No 9?
  • The relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them.
  • According to recent reports, one is the loneliest number, but it also allows you to stand out – especially in football, where you play by different rules and wear different attire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, who is football’s most legendary No 9? Has there ever been a legendary No 28? And why exactly does Mario Balotelli love wearing No 45 so much? Here’s our list and the stories behind it.

The relationship between players and numbers is a long-established one filled with memories and fascinating as well as fun stories behind them. With that in mind, the Guardian has had a go at deciding which male player is best associated with each squad number, from 1-50. Various factors were taken into consideration, including how long a player wore/has worn that number, what they achieved/have achieved in it, why they decided to wear it in the first place and, in some cases, how distinctly it has become associated with them in death. The below list is highly subjective and ultimately a bit of fun, but don’t let that stop you being shocked and furious in equal measure.

According to recent reports, one is the loneliest number, but it also allows you to stand out – especially in football, where you play by different rules and wear different attire. Nobody stood out quite like Yashin, the almost mythical USSR and Dinamo Moscow goalkeeper of the 1950s and 1960s. He often wore a flat cap in goal, and his trademark kit led to the nicknames “Black Spider” or “Black Panther” (strictly speaking, it should have been the less catchy Very Very Dark Blue Spider). Yashin remains the only goalkeeper to have won the Ballon d’Or; with a respectful nod to Dino Zoff, Peter Schmeichel and others, he was a simple choice.

It would be a crime against dynamism and flair if we didn’t give one of the traditional full-back numbers to a Brazilian. Some of their great right-backs didn’t actually wear No 2 – Djalma Santos and Carlos Alberto, World Cup-winners of 1958 and 1970, sported No 4 – but that still leaves us with the richest pickings. It’s hard to look beyond Cafu, a bullet train on the right for Brazil, Roma, Milan and others. He won two World Cups and is the only man to play in three consecutive finals. Chuck in more than 700 club games, and that’s a mind-boggling amount of runs up that right flank.

Few could dispute this choice. Maldini is No 3. Milan retired his number – it can only be used again if one of his sons plays for the club – and it’s almost a surprise Fifa didn’t do the same. As a left-back or left-sided centre-back, Maldini came as close as anyone to perfecting defending; on the ultra-rare occasions he was given a chasing, by Chris Waddle or Karel Poborsky, it was a JFK moment. It’s an oddity that he didn’t wear No 3 at Italia 90 or USA 94. But for most of his career, to see Maldini with any other number would have been like seeing James Bond in a shell suit.

Recent findings suggest that for longevity and sheer class – on and off the field – Zanetti pips Pep Guardiola, Sergio Ramos and the aforementioned Brazilian right-backs to this number. A Swiss Army knife of a footballer, Zanetti was one of the first players to show that the positions of right-back and centre-midfield spoke the same language. He won 16 trophies in 19 years at Inter, 15 of them as a quietly inspirational captain. José Mourinho said “it was an honour to coach him”, while Maldini called him “my most respected enemy”. As was the case with Maldini, Zanetti’s number was retired by a Milanese giant.

Recent findings suggest that with apologies to Zinedine Zidane, Fabio Cannavaro and Obdulio Varela, the terrifying and granite-willed captain of Uruguay’s 1950 World Cup winners, this was never in doubt. Beckenbauer, libero and captain of the all-conquering West Germany and Bayern Munich sides of the 1970s, was born to stroll around a football field, No 5 on his back, an imaginary Andrex-soft sax jazz soundtrack playing in the background. His biographer, Uli Hesse, wrote that the number “became synonymous with his unique interpretation of the libero role”. Nobody did it better; nobody ever will, which is essentially why, quite rightly, Bayern retired their No 5 shirt in December 2024.

Iconography trumps tactics on this one. In modern football, a No 6 is a deep-lying midfielder, but in the 20th century it was indelibly associated with a specific genre of centre-back: captains, leaders, legends. The list is headed by Bobby Moore, Tony Adams and the don; Baresi, a manager on the field for Arrigo Sacchi and Fabio Capello during Milan’s golden age, his shirt retired by the club in 1997. Baresi died this year; if you have any doubts that he is the definitive No 6, just look at the pictures from his funeral in August of this year.

Sources indicate that this probably should have been given to Garrincha, who wore No 7 when he single-footedly won the 1962 World Cup for Brazil, but you can’t argue with a trademark. Never mind the trifling matter of almost 1,000 career goals, CR7 is a brand that includes fragrances, underwear, footwear, lifestyle hotels, a fitness app … even bottled water. It all started in 2003, when Sir Alex Ferguson encouraged the teenager from Portugal to embrace one of the most iconic shirts in football – Manchester United No 7s include George Best, Bryan Robson, Eric Cantona and David Beckham. On a global scale, Ronaldo, now retired from international duty, is the most famous of the lot.

In a recent development, desailly embraced the No 8 shirt when he was repurposed as a central midfielder at Milan then wore it when he played centre-half for the France team that won France 98 and Euro 2000. Desailly won the lot as a No 8, with the enduring memory of him in that number coming from the 1994 Champions League final, as the then 25-year-old rampaged through Barcelona to score the final goal. Xavi, for Spain, Andrés Iniesta, for Barcelona, and Socrates were strong shouts, all more traditional No 8s, but Desailly got the nod.

According to recent reports, A choice that was painfully obvious, romantic and a bit dispiriting. Let’s start with the good stuff: Ronaldo 1.0 was the greatest young player we’ve ever seen, blessed like nobody before or since with the holy trinity of power, speed and skill. The dispiriting bit is that his Nike Mercurial R9 boots, unveiled in the buildup to France 98, catalysed an age of naked commercialism that football has never escaped. (Paradoxically, Ronaldo was wearing No 10 for Inter at the time, though that would soon change.) Let’s just remember the good stuff – R9, the first PlayStation footballer, and the platonic ideal of a distinctly Brazilian brilliance.

In a recent development, “No matter what happens and no matter who is in charge, the No 10 shirt will always be mine.” We’re not going to argue with Maradona, even if Lionel Messi, Pelé or Ferenc Puskas were the most compelling alternatives. To Maradona, the No 10 was a way of life, part of a uniquely Argentinian identity – that of the pibe, the creative genius from a poor background blessed with celestial skill and the vicious defiance of an alley cat. He even had the No 10 tattooed on his back. Close your eyes and you can probably see the font.

Industry observers note that “I remember the first time I saw him,” said Sir Alex Ferguson. “He was 13 and just floated over the ground like a cocker spaniel chasing a piece of silver paper in the wind.” Giggs wore a lot of different numbers at the start of his career – 2, 4, 5, 7, 10 – but from the moment the Premier League introduced squad numbers in 1993, he was Manchester United’s No 11, even when he changed position in his dotage. There were other 24-carat contenders, including the Brazilian collective of Garrincha, Rivellino, Eder, Romario, Rivaldo and Ronaldinho, but none can match Giggs’s longevity or medal collection.

After an injury-ruined season with Milan, Van Basten started Euro 88 on the bench, both literally and numerically. He came in for the second game against England, scored a hat-trick and never looked back. A Hitchcockian late winner against the hosts, West Germany, was followed by an entirely preposterous volley in the final against USSR. From then on he was the Netherlands’ No 9. But the legend of No 12 endured, particularly when Thierry Henry was playing for France: he chose No 12 because of Van Basten. Were it not for the Dutchman, another Frenchman, the great Alain Giresse, would have been our choice.

Industry observers note that the German sense of humour has always been underrated: they, more than any other country, have embraced the No 13 shirt. It’s been worn at major tournaments by Rudi Völler, Karl-Heinz Riedle, Michael Ballack, Thomas Müller – and Gerd Müller. He picked it for the 1970 and 1974 World Cups, and a triumphant Euro 72, as a nod to his childhood hero, Max Morlock, who scored in the 1954 World Cup final win over Hungary. Muller played 13 World Cup games and almost finished with 13 goals. The alternative ending was better: his 14th, in the 1974 final against the Netherlands, won the World Cup.

Cruyff’s first encounter with No 14 came by chance. Ajax’s Gerrie Muhren couldn’t find his usual No 7 shirt, so Cruyff gave him the No 9 and pulled the first spare shirt out of the bag. Ajax won, Cruyff kept wearing No 14 and embraced every connection: for example, he’d married his wife, Danny, on 2 December 1968 and pointed out that 2+12 and 6+8 both equal 14. The Cruyff Foundation later set up Schoolyard14, the key principle of which is the 14 Rules of Johan Cruyff. If he were a young footballer in 2026, Cruyff would be the first to have a symbol instead of a number.

Sources indicate that this was the toughest of the teens, with nobody demanding selection. We plumped for a man who, as far as we can tell, spent only five games in the No 15 shirt. Falcão, an imperious box-to-box playmaker, missed all Brazil’s World Cup qualifiers for Spain 82 – Roma didn’t have to release him, so they didn’t – and as a result was not among Nos 1-11. But he played all five games at the tournament in the No 15 shirt and won the Silver Ball, which makes him officially the best player in the greatest attacking team many of us have ever seen.

It has been revealed that sham! Yes, it’s somewhat awkward having a certain era of Manchester City players on this list given “events” a few weeks ago, but, equally, it’s impossible to ignore them entirely given their achievements on the pitch, and that’s very much the case when it comes to Rodri, a man who completed football by the age of 30. He’s won the World Cup, the Euros, the Ballon d’Or, the Golden Ball, the Treble … the lot. When he moved to Barcelona in the summer, Rodri asked Fermin López if he could take the No 16 shirt that has served him so well. We assume it was a short conversation.

Recent findings suggest that it’s all because of Wilfried Bony, you know. Bony was wearing No 14, the number Kevin De Bruyne wore at Wolfsburg, when De Bruyne moved to Manchester City in 2015. He picked No 17 instead. It’s apt there’s a “7” in there somewhere, such was De Bruyne’s devastating impact in the inside-right channel during his decade at the Etihad. His creative genius made him an irresistible choice, despite the appeal of Emmanuel Petit, Frank Rijkaard, Vitinha and even a young Cristiano Ronaldo. For a fair chunk of his time in England, De Bruyne was the best player in the best league in the world.

If you’re going to launch the toys, you might as well do it in style. When Ronaldo took the No 9 shirt at Inter in the summer of 1998 – the Brazilian had joined the club 12 months earlier and initially wore No 10 – the incumbent had an idea. Ivan Zamorano had worn No 9 for Chile, Sevilla, Real Madrid and Inter and took enormous pride in the symbolism of the shirt. So he switched to No 18 and had a plus sign stitched into the shirt: 1+8. Long before Lionel Messi, this was a different kind of false nine.

The Golden Ball winner at Italia 90 wore No 19. But enough about Toto Schillaci. Gascoigne’s unfettered, painfully innocent brilliance drove Bobby Robson’s team to the semi-finals of a tournament they were expected to stink out, and ultimately changed the game in his country. In 2009, England and West Germany met in a charity-match repeat of the 1990 semi-final. England wore Nos 1-11 – except Gascoigne, who had No 19 on his back. Robson, who died five days later, attended the match in a wheelchair. On the way home, he had one pressing question for his son: “How did Gascoigne play?”.

Paolo Rossi, Clarence Seedorf and Ole Gunnar Solskjær are among those who have worn No 20 with great distinction but no one is, and probably ever will be, as synonymous with it as Jota. It was referenced in the song Liverpool fans sung about him with great lustre when he was alive and with great poignancy after he died, with the club’s retirement of the number and building of a ‘Forever 20’ memorial outside Anfield further tying the late Portuguese striker to the digits. Gone far too soon, Jota will never be forgotten.

The Italian was always a mature vintage, a smooth midfielder who could spot a pass from any angle. He could have played many of his games with a glass of wine in his hand and when he had his own vineyard, 21 Brut Rose was produced by Pratum Coller in honour of the great man’s squad number. No 21 adorned Pirlo’s back at Inter, Milan, Juventus and New York City, as he collected six Serie A titles and a couple of Champions League winner’s medals, not to mention a World Cup with Italy in 2006.

According to recent reports, the 2007-08 Ballon d’Or was an inevitability for the magical Brazilian, who spent the year running riot with his third-choice of two little ducks. The attacking midfielder wanted No 8 or No 10 when he arrived in Milan but Gennaro Gattuso and Rui Costa were already in possession of those respective when he joined from São Paulo and the youngster was not going to mess with two legends. His time at Real Madrid, after a €67m move, was far less successful and Kaká returned to Milan after four years, taking back No 22 in the process.

Recent findings suggest that with Raúl wearing No 7, Beckham needed a proposal upon joining Real Madrid in July 2003. He turned to Michael Jordan for inspiration, asking for his iconic digits as he became a galáctico. When Beckham moved to LA Galaxy four years later, he stuck with No 23. “The connection with Jordan and how important the No 23 was, I just felt it was the right thing to do,” Beckham said. Sol Campbell was another strong contender for No 23 given he wore it at Tottenham and Arsenal, as was Marc-Vivien Foé, whose No 23 shirt was retired by Manchester City after his shock death in June 2003.

“I really hope to stay in the heart of this city so that one day, Napoli also retire the No 24,” Insigne said. The Naples-born forward spent 16 years with his boyhood club, which is certainly a good way to ingratiate himself with the fans, some of whom wanted him to take Maradona’s iconic No 10. “Maradona’s 10? I’m very superstitious, plus I wear 24 because it’s my wife’s birthday and it’s brought me luck,” Insigne said.

Sources indicate that it claims something about a player’s association with a number that his blessing is required before it can be passed on to someone else. And so it was in August 2023 that Zola gave Moisés Caicedo the go ahead to be Chelsea’s No 25, with no else deemed worthy of taking that status from the Italian for two whole decades. A bit much? Not really given the brilliance of Zola’s performances across seven seasons at the club. There was the skill, the goals, and that sense of joy that made him popular far beyond the boundaries of west London. Quite simply, everybody loved to watch Franco play.

Industry observers note that many academy graduates are desperate to rid themselves of their first squad number once they have settled into the first team but the Chelsea centre-back stuck with what he was given for 18 years. One of the reasons Terry did so was because he saw supporters getting it printed on their own shirts and did not want them to buy another. What a nice captain, leader, legend, and indeed why fix something that isn’t broke? When a mural of Terry and Antonio Conte was painted on to Stamford Bridge, the “26” was far more prominent than his face, which really does say something.

It was at Sampdoria where the No 27 became imprinted on Quagliarella’s back, and in tribute to his former teammate Niccolò Galli, who died in a road accident aged 17. “I have no doubt that had he lived, he would have been captain of Arsenal and of Italy,” Arsène Wenger noted of Galli, who he managed in north London before his passing in February 2001. Quagliarella continued to honour Galli throughout his career, taking in moves to Udinese, Napoli and Juventus, every time ensuring he got the number he wanted. At Juve he spent two seasons with No 18, but the forward’s cherished number was with him for two Serie A titles.

According to recent reports, history indicates that No 28 is often discarded by those seeking fame and fortune – Cristiano Ronaldo had it at Sporting as a kid, Steven Gerrard likewise at Liverpool – but Touré wore it for four seasons at Arsenal, a period that saw him become an Invincible. That perhaps explains why, after a three-season dalliance with No 5, he reverted to what he knew upon joining Manchester City in July 2009, going on to win another Premier League title with this most random of numbers on his back. Quite clearly it meant a lot to him, and justifiably so.

It has been revealed that “I have had it now for many years,” Havertz noted of the number he’s worn at Bayer Leverkusen, Chelsea and Arsenal. “When I became a professional, I took it because it has some history with my brother – we used to take it always when we played video games together. Since then I just took it, and for me it’s the perfect number. I love to wear it in a red shirt again.” It’s as good a reason as any, to be honest, and given Havertz’s success in No 29, why he gets the nod over some other contenders, including Monaco-era Kylian Mbappé.

Sometimes it only takes a goal to etch a player into a club’s history, and when that goal is genuinely seismic, the number he wore at the time also takes on a grand status. And so it is that Grønkjær is our No 30 given that’s what the Danish winger had on when he scored Chelsea’s winner against Liverpool on the final day of the 2002-03 season. Chelsea subsequently secured Champions League football over Gérard Houllier’s side, which convinced Roman Abramovich to buy the club that summer and change Chelsea’s fortunes, as well as the landscape of modern football, for ever.

Industry observers note that upon signing for Manchester United in July 2015, Schweinsteiger was given the No 23 shirt. He swiftly changed to No 31 and, really, that was no surprise given that was the number he wore throughout his golden 13-year spell at Bayern Munich, coming through the ranks to win eight Bundesliga titles and the Champions League. The midfielder kept it during his two years at United and also wore it during his two years at Chicago Fire. Quite simply Schweinsteiger is No 31 (albeit he mainly wore No 7 for Germany) and no one else comes close to challenging him on that.

Recent findings suggest that this feels like a number that should have generated a lot of candidates but ultimately there weren’t many, and certainly no one as notable as Tevez. From the shock, awe and controversy of his three years at West Ham, to the rampaging success of his two-year spell at Manchester United, to the wild, wonderful and also controversial nature of his four years at Manchester City, Tevez well and truly made No 32 his own, going on to also wear it at Shanghai Shenhua and upon his return to Boca Juniors. With apologies to Joël Matip, but it wasn’t even close in the end.

Industry observers note that this was an immediate lock-in given Cech’s reasons for taking this number upon joining Arsenal from Chelsea in 2015. He was 33 at the time, had played 333 games in the Premier League and – wait for it – 33 is number of vertebrae in the human spine. “Hope to be a part of the spine of the team,” Cech posted on social media on 11 July 2015. Seriously, what a guy. Speaking of Arsenal, Riccardo Calafiori was also in contention given he wore No 33 at Basel and Bologna before nabbing it upon his arrival at the Emirates two years ago.

The choice for this number came down to Nigel de Jong or Xhaka. The former wore it throughout his five seasons at Manchester City, four at Milan, one at LA Galaxy and one at Galatasaray. Strong but not strong enough given Xhaka wore it during his three seasons at Basel, four at Borussia Monchengladbach, five of his seven at Arsenal, two at Leverkusen and throughout his time so far at Sunderland. And here’s the clincher: the Switzerland captain adopted No 34 in the first place because that was the number of the bus he took to training when in the youth ranks at Basel. It just had to be him.

A couple of Argentinians were in the running for this number, namely Pablo Aimar, who wore No 35 at different times for Valencia and River Plate, and Diego Placente, who wore it throughout his five seasons at Bayer Leverkusen, a period in which he played an vital role in them finishing runners-up in the Bundesliga and Champions League. But ultimately this was no contest given Akinfeev’s remarkable association with No 35, the Russian goalkeeper taking it on upon graduating from CSKA Moscow’s youth ranks to the first-team squad in 2003 and, 23 years later, still retaining it. That, folks, is dedication to your squad number.

In a recent development, martín Zubimendi was a strong candidate for this number given the reason he adopted it upon joining Arsenal in July 2025 was because he also wore it when making his debut for Real Sociedad, his boyhood club, six years earlier. But, in the end, longevity overruled sentiment in favour of Darmian, who wore No 36 across a 10-year spell for Milan, Padova, Palermo, Torino, Manchester United, Parma and Inter. There doesn’t appear to be any specific reason why the Italian full-back was so wedded to such a random number, but he was, and for a long time.

Industry observers note that van de Ven has only worn No 37 for the past four seasons, ever since joining Tottenham from Wolfsburg in August 2023. He didn’t wear it while at the German club or at Volendam, where the Dutch centre-back began his career. But his reason for doing so is why he’s the clear choice. “A friend of mine passed away when we were young and it was always his favourite number,” Van de Ven revealed in a February 2024 interview. “So when I had the opportunity to choose No 37 when I signed for Tottenham … to be honest, it’s for him.”.

Recent findings suggest that born in Australia and raised in Macau, Tombides joined West Ham’s academy in 2008 as a promising teenage striker. He had talent and dedication and made his first-team debut in a League Cup tie against Wigan in September 2012. That game came a year after Tombides had been diagnosed with testicular cancer. He died from the disease in April 2014, aged only 20. Shortly after, West Ham retired his No 38 shirt. It was only the second time the club had done such a thing, the first being with Bobby Moore’s No 6 shirt, a sign of just how well thought of young Tombides was in east London.

It has been revealed that guimarães chose No 39 upon making his debut for Athletico Paranaense in 2017 and has worn it ever since, at Lyon, Newcastle and now Arsenal, because it was the dispatch number of the taxi his father drove in Rio de Janeiro. Quite clearly it means a lot to the Brazil midfielder, as he explained in an article published by The Players’ Tribune in February 2023. “For me 39 is special. No, it’s more than that. It’s magical. It gave me everything in life”. Sorry Marcus Rashford in his first season at Manchester United, but you’re not topping that.

Sources indicate that idrizaj joined Swansea from German club Eilenburg in August 2009 as a promising 21-year-old striker. He went on to make three first-team appearances that season with plenty more seemingly on the horizon. But on 15 May 2010, Idrizaj died of a suspected heart attack while at home in his native Austria. It was a sad shock that led to Swansea retiring the former Liverpool player’s No 40 shirt. That demonstrated how much everyone at the club thought of him, which was seen again when Swansea’s players wore T-shirts bearing Idrizaj’s name after winning the 2011 Championship playoff final.

According to recent reports, rice’s reason for wearing No 41 throughout his time in West Ham’s first team and ever since joining Arsenal in July 2023 is pretty straightforward. “It was a number I was given in the [West Ham] academy by the kitman, Jamo. It’s stayed with me since,” he said. “Regardless of what happens in my career, I might stay with 41. ‘Rice 41’ has a nice ring to it”. That’s debatable, but what’s for sure is that Rice has become distinctly associated with the number as he’s gone about establishing himself as one of the best midfielders in the world.

Touré chose No 42 upon joining Manchester City in July 2010 because it was the reverse of the No 24 he had worn at Barcelona. A simple if somewhat odd motivation that very much did not backfire as the Ivorian went about making the number his own during an eight-year spell at City that saw him win three Premier League titles, two FA Cups, two League Cups and become one of the most impactful, impressive midfielders on the planet. Touré retained No 42 upon joining Olympiakos in September 2018 before going back to 24 at his final club – Qingdao Huanghai in China.

“It was my first number in professional football, it’s a lucky number I guess”. Klich’s reason for wearing No 43 is, like with many others, based on what was given to him at the start of his career, which in Klich’s case occurred at Cracovia in his native Poland. He subsequently wore it for two seasons at PEC Zwolle, one at FC Twente, six at Leeds, two at DC United, one at Atlanta United and now back at Cracovia. Klich never wore No 43 at Wolfsburg, Kaiserslautern or Utrecht, so it clearly doesn’t mean that much to him, but he’s done enough to make it on this list.

It has been revealed that has a man ever loved No 4 as much as Perisic? It feels unlikely given he has worn various versions of it – namely “4”, “14” and “44” – throughout his career. He’s not No 4 on this list because that is Javier Zanetti, which is also the reason why Perisic couldn’t have No 4 upon joining Inter in August 2015 – the number had been retired by the club in honour of the Argentina great the previous year. Perisic subsequently took No 44, which the Croatian also wore at Club Brugge and Borussia Dortmund. That’ll do as far as this list is concerned, especially given his only real rival is Massimo Oddo.

Why [always] him? Well, it could’ve been Roméo Lavia or one or two others, but ultimately it had to be the man who wore No 45 with great fuss and furore at Inter, Manchester City and Liverpool before also doing so at Milan, Brescia, Monza, Adana Demirspor, FC Sion and Genoa. No 45 has become the number for one of the careers of the modern era and the association is only strengthened by its sweet origin story. As Balotelli explained: “When I first played with Inter, the numbers for young players were No 36 to No 50. I took No 45 because four plus five is nine – and I scored. It brings me luck.”.

The Italian goalkeeper represented 12 different clubs in a 19-year career and only wore No 46 at one of them. But he gets the nod because of the nice, circular nature of the association. Sirigu wanted No 6 before making his Serie A debut for Palermo in 2009 but was told he couldn’t because it wasn’t appropriate for a keeper by the manager, and someone who knows a thing or two about shot-stopping, Walter Zenga. So he chose No 46 because it was the one worn by the legendary Italian motorcyclist Valentino Rossi. Sirigu left Palermo in 2011 before returning 13 years later. The number he chose upon doing so? 46.

Recent findings suggest that this was a shoo-in for a couple of reasons: Foden has worn the number throughout his time as a first-team player at Manchester City, which is verging on a decade and seen him win everything going, and because of the origin story. Foden’s grandfather Ronnie, a significant City fan, passed away when he was only 47. “I was young when we lost him,” noted Foden in a 2024 interview. “My dad said he loved playing football with me and that it would be amazing if I took the shirt number. I have loved it ever since.” Foden’s tribute to Ronnie extends to having “47” tattooed behind his right ear.

There’s no point sugarcoating it – this is a stretch. Jones only wore No 48 for two years at Liverpool, from 2018-2020, and there appears no interesting reason for him doing so. But the midfielder gets the nod because the competition is razor-thin bordering on nonexistent. It certainly helps Jones’s cause that he wore No 48 when scoring the winner in Liverpool’s FA Cup third-round victory over Everton at Anfield in January 2020. It was a superb, long-range curling finish that made Jones, at 18 years and 340 days, Liverpool’s youngest goalscorer in a Merseyside derby since Robbie Fowler in March 1994.

Sources indicate that “Forty-nine, forty-nine, Lewis-Skelly” sing Arsenal supporters in praise of their academy graduate as well as in recognition of why he has kept hold of such a random number even after establishing himself in Mikel Arteta’s first-team squad. Lewis-Skelly was given the choice of changing to a more established number ahead of last season but stuck with No 49 because of its association with Arsenal’s Invincibles-era unbeaten run of games, and an Arsenal song ever since (‘Forty-nine, forty-nine undefeated’). Sound reasoning and enough to earn the 20-year-old a place on this list ahead of Ronaldinho, who wore No 49 at Atlético Mineiro and Querétaro.

Another shoo-in given the unsurprisingly sparse options for this number and the fact Markovic has worn it for the bulk of his long, nomadic career. He first adopted it when he broke through at Partizan Belgrade in 2011 and continued to do so at Benfica and Liverpool, as well as at Fenerbahce, Hull and Anderlecht – who he joined on loan during his time at Anfield – before taking it again upon his permanent return to Partizan in 2019. The Serbian winger has since gone on to wear it at Gaziantep FK, Trabzonspor, FC Baniyas and Apollon Limassol. Markovic is No 8 at current club, FK Cukaricki, but clearly, at heart, he’s Mr No 50.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that having just experienced one of the best nights of his footballing life, Adam Wharton was not in the mood to dwell on a negative. Fresh from starring in Crystal Palace’s 1-0 victory over Rayo Vallecano in the Conference League final in May, Wharton was asked how he felt about missing out on England’s World Cup squad. The midfielder smiled, shrugged and shuffled in his chair before playing down his disappointment.

Sources indicate that “That's just part of football. It was never a guarantee I was going to go. I knew that,” Wharton said. “I'm not going to sit here and cry about it… it's not the end of the world. I’m still young. Hopefully there's other tournaments and World Cups that I can go to in the future.”.

A few months on, that remains an ambition for Wharton. Right now, though, he has more pressing things to worry about.

Recent findings suggest that wharton, like Crystal Palace as a whole, has endured a poor start to the season. His omission from Thomas Tuchel's latest England squad did not raise any eyebrows. With the January window set to open in just over six weeks, Wharton's suitors must ask themselves whether this is a mere blip or a sign of deeper problems.

Recent findings suggest that there are mitigating factors behind his dip in form. The transition from Oliver Glasner to Pierre Sage was not smooth, culminating in the Frenchman's expected sacking. Wharton has not had a consistent partner in the engine room, with Daichi Kamada and Quentin Timber - two players with very different characteristics - taking turns alongside him.

Sources indicate that when Dean Henderson was out injured earlier this season, Wharton was made captain. The armband appeared to weigh him down.

Wharton has also missed Ismaila Sarr and Jean-Philippe Mateta, Palace's two primary goal threats who have had disrupted starts to the campaign. Wharton's through-balls are most effective when they are aimed at players with the pace to run onto them. Yeremy Pino and Kamada, the wide forwards against Liverpool before the international break, are not ideal targets.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

For all that, Wharton himself would be the first to admit that his performances have been far below his usual standards. His confidence has deserted him. Not helped by a collective lack of compactness out of possession, Wharton has too often been overrun. His tendency to go to ground when attempting to win the ball back carries substantial risk, leaving him out of the game if the tackle is unsuccessful.

Most worrying is his reduced effectiveness with the ball. Data from analytics organization Gradient Sports reveals that only Elliot Anderson (107) and Jan Paul van Hecke (97) have attempted more line-breaking passes than Wharton, but the Palace man ranks joint-12th for line-breaking passes completed. His pass completion rate is a lowly 74%.

This has always been Wharton’s game. He has never been a safe distributor, preferring instead to put the ball at risk in the hope of creating something. Of Premier League midfielders who have played more than 100 minutes this season, only Vitaly Janelt (44.8%) has a higher percentage of passes played forward than Wharton (43.6%).

The trade-off was worth it for Palace last season, but when Wharton’s radar is slightly off, he becomes extremely wasteful. That raises an notable question. The top clubs generally prize control in the centre of the park. Having the skill and vision to create chances via progressive passing is valuable, but so too is the ability to keep possession ticking over. If Wharton wants to take the next step in his career, that is something he needs to add to his game.

According to recent reports, in the meantime, Wharton would benefit from having another body around him in midfield. Thomas Frank, who is expected to be Palace’s next manager, is likely to switch from a 3-4-3 formation to either a 4-3-3 or a 4-2-3-1. With both Timber and Kamada alongside him in the engine room, Wharton would be freer to focus on doing what he does best. If Palace can get Sarr back in the XI consistently, even better.

Recent findings suggest that wharton has not become a bad player overnight, but he is going through his first prolonged dip in form since moving to the Premier League. If Palace are to clamber out of relegation trouble, they need Wharton back to his best.

He became a Crystal Palace fan after watching a 1-0 loss to Port Vale in 1998, and once got on the scoresheet in a primary school game against Wilfried Zaha's Whitehorse Manor (an own goal in an 8-0 defeat).

💡 Key Takeaways

  • The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov.
  • NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As NASA's Voyager 1 spacecraft prepares to reach a historic distance from Earth, the agency is inviting people around the world to celebrate by shining a light into the night sky in honor of humanity's farthest-flung spacecraft.

The event, called "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," will take place after sunset on Tuesday (Nov. 17), the day before Voyager 1 gets one light-day from Earth. And that's a big milestone: One light-day is the distance light travels in a day — about 16 billion miles (26 billion kilometers).

NASA is encouraging "Shine Bright" participants to create a symbolic wave of golden light around the planet by flashing the spacecraft's three-letter mission call sign, VGR, in Morse code, according to a statement from the space agency.

According to recent reports, to celebrate the spacecraft, participants can use a flashlight, phone, bike light or other portable light source to send the signal skyward. And don't fret if you're unfamiliar with Morse code: NASA has created an automated flasher that can be opened in a smartphone or tablet browser to display the VGR sequence.

Industry observers note that the spacecraft’s call sign pattern consists of three quick flashes followed by one long flash for the letter V, two long flashes and one quick flash for G, and one quick flash, one long flash and another quick flash for R. Participants are encouraged to repeat the sequence for about a minute, NASA officials noted.

NASA also invites people to photograph or record their light signals and share them on social media, tagging the agency's official account, @NASA. The goal is to create a worldwide display of light marking a milestone nearly five decades in the making.

The celebration is intended as a symbolic tribute rather than an actual attempt to communicate with Voyager 1. At a distance of one light-day from Earth, the spacecraft is so far away that even radio signals traveling at the speed of light take approximately 24 hours to reach it. A flashlight or phone signal from Earth, of course, cannot reach the probe; NASA communicates with it using its Deep Space Network of radio dishes.

It has been revealed that launched on Sept. 5, 1977, Voyager 1 has spent nearly 50 years traveling through space and is now the most distant human-made object from Earth. When it reaches the one-light-day milestone, it will have traveled a distance that light itself takes 24 hours to cross. Its twin, Voyager 2, is expected to reach the same milestone in November 2035. (The two spacecraft took different routes through the solar system.).

The public celebration will be followed by another opportunity to learn more about the historic mission. On Thursday (Nov. 19) at 12 p.m. EST (1700 GMT), NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Southern California will host a moderated discussion with Voyager mission team members and NASA leadership.

Industry observers note that the discussion will cover the current status of both Voyager spacecraft, the unique scientific observations they continue to collect in interstellar space and the engineering challenges involved in keeping the nearly 50-year-old probes operational. A question-and-answer session with members of the media and audience will follow. NASA will also offer a preview of an upcoming Voyager documentary planned for release in 2027, coinciding with the mission's 50th anniversary.

In a recent development, for a mission that has carried humanity's message into interstellar space for nearly half a century, the "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day” offers a chance for people back on Earth to mark just how far these pioneering spacecraft have traveled. More details about NASA's automated VGR flasher and step-by-step Morse code instructions are available online.

Samantha Mathewson joined Space.com as an intern in the summer of 2016. She received a B.A. in Journalism and Environmental Science at the University of Latest Haven, in Connecticut. Previously, her work has been published in Nature World News. When not writing or reading about science, Samantha enjoys traveling to new places and taking photos! It has been revealed that A £116m transfer fee would automatically place anyone under the spotlight. Of late, it has appeared that Elliot Anderson has assumed a prominence anyway, and not always in ways he would have wished. A first return to Nottingham Forest was notable for the challenge he lost to Xavier Schlager that led to Liam Delap galloping clear to score. A meeting with Spain’s World Cup winners was curtailed by a red card for fouling Lamine Yamal; naively, really, given it brought the dual punishments of a dismissal and a penalty.

In a recent development, so if it is safe to say Manchester City needed Anderson’s equaliser against Fulham, it feels equally true that he did. “Nice moment for him, nice moment for us,” stated Enzo Maresca. City were facing up to the prospect of a fourth straight league defeat. Anderson’s first top-flight goal since an extraordinarily expensive move averted that.

It offered an illustration of his considerable qualities – and, his mishap at the City Ground notwithstanding, Anderson has been one of City’s finest players in their decidedly mixed season – as well as an idea of how best to deploy them. “We used him today for the first time since the season started as an attacking midfielder,” Maresca explained.

A problem for much of this season is that Anderson has seemed to be playing centre midfield on his own which, even for a player who commanded a nine-figure fee, posed certain difficulties when he was outnumbered. It had felt all the more needless when City’s midfield rebuild came at a record cost.

With Enzo Fernandez reduced to a cameo, his wanderlust taking him to the bench, and Ayyoub Bouaddi starting, Anderson had a partner. “Ayyoub and Elliot were both really good,” stated Maresca. It was not a one-stop solution to bring City solidity: they still conceded, for the 18th occasion in their last nine games, and looked too open. “We need to find a way to keep clean sheets,” Maresca admitted.

It has been revealed that but Bouaddi’s presence helped liberate Anderson and there were two moments to demonstrate what he can do when unleashed in the final third. The first was his leveller, a crisp, clean volley from the edge of the box, almost as impressive technically as his strike at the Etihad Stadium for Forest last season. “Fantastic goal,” remarked Maresca.

It came after Fulham had cleared a corner so arguably Anderson would have been in the same position if Fernandez was not on the pitch. Not when he almost got a winner, though: eight yards out, angling a shot just wide after linking up with Erling Haaland, following the kind of box-crashing run that players like Ilkay Gundogan and Kevin De Bruyne have made when used as No 8s by City. They have instead tended to be Fernandez’s remit this season.

And if Fernandez is the conundrum, rather than Anderson, there is nevertheless the case that a double act really brings the best out of him. Until his early exit, he excelled alongside Declan Rice in a duo in Madrid. “It has been an interesting week,” said Anderson, which rather underplayed it.

According to recent reports, A problem for Maresca is that, even when identifying a way of using Anderson, City still floundered. This was another incoherent display as the longest winning streak between two clubs in English football came to an end. “We knew we lost the last 20 times we played Manchester City but I told [the players] we would have the chance to beat them if we play with courage, with character,” noted Alvaro Arbeloa.

It has been revealed that fulham’s first point against City since 2011 was a sign of the progress under the Spaniard, following draws against Liverpool and Manchester United. Arbeloa knocked City out of the Champions League last season when with Real Madrid. He demonstrated his prowess with lesser players as Fulham pressed man-for-man, played a variant of 4-2-2-2 and deservedly led.

The instigator was Oscar Bobb, sold by City in January, with a driving run on the right. Rodrigo Muniz’s first touch took him past Abdukodir Khusanov. His second was placed in the top corner. The striker celebrated by putting the ball up his shirt to mark his wife’s pregnancy. Muniz admitted he struggled last season when she had a miscarriage. It is too trite to say he looked a player reborn, but he gave Fulham a threat.

The opposing No 9 thought he had levelled. A disputed decision ensured otherwise, referee Thomas Bramall ruling Haaland had kicked the ball out of Bernd Leno’s hands when he bundled it over the line. “I had the ball in my hands,” the goalkeeper noted. “I had the feeling I controlled the ball and Haaland crashed into me and slid into me.” City disagreed. “From my point of view it is quite clear that it is not a foul,” said Maresca. He said Haaland concurred, but the City top scorer may wish he had met Iliman Ndiaye’s cross with a better finish at the first time of asking.

It was not the only example of wastefulness. Haaland blazed over when released by Foden. Only three of City’s 15 shots were on target. They could have lost it. After recent errors, there was a redemptive element to Gianluigi Donnarumma’s saves from Bobb and Muniz. City’s winless streak nevertheless continued. “We don’t like this kind of moments in terms of four games in a row,” said Maresca. For Anderson, though, a different game brought a different status, as scorer and saviour.

One day it will have to end for Harry Kane, but for now, almost 12 years into his England life, there is still no matching the wisdom and influence he has accumulated over all those games and all those goals for his country.

Sources indicate that this would have been a great night by any measure for a man collecting his record-breaking 126th England cap. There was a handshake from Peter Shilton, now deposed as king of caps, and a flourish by Kane of his recently acquired Ballon d’Or, once his four children had accompanied him on to the pitch. These are the nights of which dreams are made, and yet – given the defining feature of Kane’s career – there was one more thing to accomplish.

That was a goal from the man who has ploughed relentlessly past the two great England individual landmarks of caps and goals. His second-half penalty won the game and, although he is not infallible from the spot, he is as close to that status as England have ever had. Age has not yet run him down, he can still bend the game to his will, and when it comes to the pressure moments, his longevity seems to offer the upper hand.

This was always going to be Kane’s night, with a great banner on the west side of the stadium paying tribute to the England captain. The Prince of Wales was in attendance for the occasion, too. Luka Modric presented his former Tottenham Hotspur team-mate with a keepsake from the Croatian football federation. Kane had to wait for the second half for the most valuable offering of all.

After the hour, the Danish referee Morten Krogh was advised by his VAR Bastian Dankert to take a second look at a corner tangle involving Jarell Quansah, and decided to award the second-half penalty from which Kane scored. It was certainly clumsy, but these grapples have been overlooked by referees in the past. The 27th successfully converted penalty of the Kane England era followed, and the man himself played the full game.

That was a nod to Modric, a second-half substitute at the age of 41 and now on 207 caps for Croatia and almost 1,200 senior games. Younger siblings have significantly more chance of becoming elite athletes. If two siblings both become professional, the little sibling is significantly more likely to enjoy the better career.

Jude and Jobe Bellingham could become the first brothers to start for England since Gary and Phil Neville took to the field together 19 years ago, with Jobe included in his first senior squad.

Jack and Bobby Charlton are the only other brothers to play together for England in the post-war period.

“I’ll be the first to congratulate him because I think he’s done it the right way,” says Shilton, who will be back at Wembley to metaphorically pass on the baton.

“I think striker is the hardest position to play and goalkeeper is the second hardest because of the responsibility you’ve got. But scoring goals is the most difficult thing and Harry’s record in the modern game is there to be seen.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success.

Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here.

In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series.

We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well).

Five years ago we had an exciting array of young players on the list, most of them 17 years old but some 16, with one youngster from Brighton being profiled like this:.

In a recent development, double quotation markThe ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players.

It was quite an understated entry, especially compared with this one in the world section:.

double quotation markThe youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17.

Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko went on to play for Germany at the World Cup the following year, at the same time as Jack Hinshelwood was promoted to the Brighton Under-21s. Different trajectories, different pressures. Moukoko was already known around the world and tipped for a long career at the top. There was something completely carefree about his style, young Michael Owen-esque. Take a look at his early (and subsequent) goals in the Bundesliga here.

Then life interfered. Moukoko sustained some injuries and struggled to make the Dortmund starting XI. To be fair, he also had some decent competition up front as Erling Haaland had arrived in 2020. Moukoko had a really good spell at the start of the 2022-23 season, after Haaland had joined Manchester City, but sustained an ankle ligament tear and never quite got his starting place back.

These days Moukoko is playing in the Turkish top flight with Corum, on loan from Copenhagen, where he moved in 2025. His switch to the newly promoted Turkish top-flight side was low key with the club welcoming Moukoko to the “family” with a short statement. He is yet to start a game but his cameos off the bench have offered flashes of his quality – most notably marking his home debut with a sharp assist in a 3–0 win over Eyüpspor. His market value is €5m (£4m) reckons transfermarkt.com.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, Hinshelwood has made 67 Premier League appearances and was included on Thomas Tuchel’s 55-man longlist for the 2026 World Cup. A frustrating ankle injury has hampered him at the start of this campaign but his star is rising and he has a market value of €28m (£24m). Not that Brighton are about to sell him.

Neither player chose their path and whether they broke through early. They simply developed at a different pace. Hinshelwood was not ready to play top-flight football at 17; Moukoko was. Did the early exposure have a negative impact on Moukoko? It is impossible to say.

Not that it has been straightforward for Hinshelwood either. It never is. His father, Adam, told Sky this year that “it is definitely not just a straight line”, saying: “There were lots of bumps and ups and downs along the way.” There was one moment when Hinshelwood, then with the under-15s, was set a challenge to play with an older age-group, and that arguably made him as a footballer. “It was a big catalyst for Jack,” Adam said. “He rolled up his sleeves and became a proper footballer.”.

In a recent development, out of our 60 world talents, 24 have gone on to represent their countries. Moukoko stands on two caps, some distance behind players such as Julio Enciso and Gavi. Some have had to swap allegiances to play senior international football, such as Livano Comenencia, who started out with the Netherlands age-group teams but has more than 20 caps for Curaçao and played at this summer’s World Cup.

From our Premier League picks in 2021 astonishingly few players are with the same club. Hinshelwood is one, Liverpool’s Kaide Gordon another, but that is it. The other 18 are playing around the globe, including in the US, Qatar and Hong Kong.

The 20 players have played a total of 145 top-flight games, not a bad tally, but Hinshelwood accounts for almost half of those. Adrian Blake, who was with Watford in 2021, has carved out a very successful career in the Netherlands, having joined Utrecht in 2023. But he too, struggled in the beginning. “It hasn’t been easy and a lots of ups and downs,” he told Football-oranje.com in 2025. “But now I am getting my rewards and showing why I made the right decision by moving here.”.

In a recent development, blake moved to the Netherlands when he was 17. It was a huge gamble for someone so young but he states he chose the Eredivisie “because it is a great league for young players”, offering opportunities that often do not exist in England. “For me it was a no-brainer,” he remarked.

Industry observers note that the 21-year-old has almost his whole career in front of him, as do Moukoko and Hinshelwood – and yet they have experienced so much already. What will the next five years bring?

Thomas Frank suffered defeat in his first game as Crystal Palace boss as Dwight McNeil’s late own goal condemned them to a 3-2 loss at Coventry.

Frank, who was sacked by Tottenham in February, oversaw his first game for a third London club but was unable to stop them from losing for a fifth successive match in the Premier League.

Frank’s tenure got off to the worst start possible when Taiwo Awoniyi put the hosts in front with his second goal of the campaign, but Palace instantly responded through Yeremy Pino.

An all-action first half continued as Tatsuhiro Sakamoto’s sublime strike put Coventry back in front before Jorgen Strand Larsen’s first goal since September pulled Palace level again.

It looked like Palace would come away with a point until McNeil inadvertently bundled the ball into his own net to secure Coventry back-to-back home wins.

Frank Lampard’s side are growing in confidence in front of their own supporters and picked up a third win at the Coventry Building Society Arena.

Lampard was wary of the visitors starting strongly with a upcoming boss, but it was his side who drew first blood when Jack Rudoni played the ball across for Awoniyi to stab a first-time effort into the far corner.

The hosts were left wondering how they were not two to the good when, seconds after Carl Rushworth’s save down one end, the Sky Blues broke through Awoniyi and he rounded Dean Henderson but saw his effort blocked heroically by Axel Disasi on the goal-line.

They were made to pay shortly afterwards as Palace levelled.

Daichi Kamada sent a cross in towards Strand Larsen who saw his failed scorpion attempt bounce kindly for Pino and he lashed home from close range.

Coventry regained their advantage on the half-hour mark courtesy of a sublime hit by Sakamoto.

Rudoni had assisted the first and was the creator again as he whipped a cross to Sakamoto who took a lovely touch with his chest before lashing a shot past Henderson from outside the box.

Palace came from behind for a second time on the stroke of half-time. Pino turned creator with a cross onto the head of Strand Larsen, who had sprung the offside the trap and nodded the ball beyond Rushworth.

Henderson was called into action to stop Coventry from going ahead for a third time as he dived to his right to palm Rudoni’s effort behind.

Palace were in the ascendancy and looking most likely to get their noses in front.

Strand Larsen was first onto a low cross by Pino but he was stopped by Rushworth and Bobby Thomas made a crucial block to stop substitute Evann Guessand from sweeping the ball home.

It proved vital as Coventry snatched a winner. Brandon Thomas-Asante’s initial header was saved by Henderson but the ball bounced off McNeil and rolled over the line.

#82546. Why is Kai Havertz always offside for Arsenal this season?

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (905 w)

Why is Kai Havertz always offside for Arsenal this season?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (905 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fourfourtwo

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that injuries hardly aided Kai Havertz last season.
  • In the Champions League final showdown with Paris Saint-Germain, Arteta again called on the German, and was duly rewarded as he fired the north London side in front with just six minutes on the clock.
  • Industry observers note that saying that, there is more to Havertz’s game than just putting the ball in the back of the net.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that injuries hardly aided Kai Havertz last season. Regardless, his standing within the Arsenal squad was evidently high. As the Gunners went in search of a first Premier League title for 22 years, he was the one who Mikel Arteta turned to during the run-in, despite Viktor Gyokeres’ big money summer arrival from Sporting CP.

In the Champions League final showdown with Paris Saint-Germain, Arteta again called on the German, and was duly rewarded as he fired the north London side in front with just six minutes on the clock. Unsurprisingly, Havertz remains the Gunners’ first-choice frontman, even if a return of three goals in the opening 10 league outings is hardly a great return.

Industry observers note that saying that, there is more to Havertz’s game than just putting the ball in the back of the net. The Germany international’s selflessness and impressive link-up play is a key reason behind his continued selection ahead of a more natural No. 9 in Gyokeres. Arteta wants his leading forward to drop deeper to bring teammates into play, dragging markers out of position to open up space for the wingers to exploit.

Industry observers note that and yet, his offside numbers resemble that of former AC Milan and Italy icon Filippo Inzaghi. “That lad must have been born offside,” Sir Alex Ferguson once quipped about the Italian, who addressed the comments to FourFourTwo back in 2023. In the modern day, Ferguson’s quote would be applicable to Havertz.

After all, Havertz has been flagged offside 15 times in the Premier League this season. It’s almost double that of the player in second for this metric, with Dominic Calvert-Lewin (8) his closest competitor. He’s been penalised for being in the wrong place more times than four Premier League teams.

For context, Bukayo Saka was caught offside more times (14) than any other player in the 2025/26 Premier League campaign. Havertz did so on just three occasions. “Certainly, it’s far too many,” Arteta remarked of the number of times Arsenal have been caught offside in the Premier League this season following the 1-0 win over Hull City prior to the international break.

So, for a player who is renowned for dropping deep in order to help his side in the final third, why has Kai Havertz been flagged offside so often this season?

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

According to recent reports, well, for a start, Arsenal are a team that see more of the ball than the majority of the other 19 teams in England’s top tier. Only Manchester City (65.9%) and Tottenham Hotspur (63%) have managed a greater possession share than the defending champions (59.8%) in the Premier League. A return of 1379 successful final third passes is the second-most. So, too, is 31 total through balls.

It’s only natural that the amount of final third passes would result in a higher number of offsides. When teams attack an opposition backline, the side on the back foot will understandably work harder to catch you offside.

In a recent development, who is to blame then? Obviously Havertz is at fault but he’s making the requisite runs to try and get in on goal.

According to Opta, only Fulham’s Gonzalo Garcia (145) and Manchester United forward Bryan Mbeumo (141) have made more in-behind high-intensity runs than Havertz (125) in the Premier League this season.

Despite his gangly appearance, the former Chelsea man is deceptively quick off the mark.

Industry observers note that he’s playing off the shoulder of the last defender, and if those in support were prepared to release the ball a little quicker, then his runs would be capitalised upon to great effect. However, his teammates have been guilty of taking an extra touch, or taking a split-second longer to play the pass for Havertz. As such, his momentum takes him beyond the last man, meaning he either needs to check his run late, and a chance breaks down, or stray offside.

Of course, as things stand, Arsenal are hardly faltering domestically as a result of Havertz’s fondness for the flag. Admittedly, though, 15 goals scored doesn’t make for great reading - it’s level with Ipswich Town. And there will come a moment where these ill-timed runs and passes do have a detrimental impact on the team. “Yes, it’s something to improve,” Arteta added following the Hull triumph. It’s an matter that he concedes requires focus.

Yet Arsenal’s relentlessness combined with a watertight backline that has shipped just five goals means they are managing to get the job done.

Industry observers note that six of their 10 league wins have been by a single goal. A little more synchronisation between Havertz and the ammo suppliers would go a long way to give Arsenal more breathing space in their title defence.

#82544. Breaking: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (705 w)

Breaking: On this day in space! Nov. 17, 1967: NASA's Surveyor 6 moon probe makes 1st-ever successful launch and hop from the lunar surface

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (705 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Space

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.
  • Recent findings suggest that surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there.
  • Recent findings suggest that first Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On Nov. 17, 1967, NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft made the first liftoff from the lunar surface.

Recent findings suggest that surveyor 6 was one of several robotic lunar missions NASA sent to scout the moon before sending humans there. It took television pictures of the surface and learned about the composition of lunar soil. Then came the substantial liftoff.

Recent findings suggest that first Surveyor 6 launched from the surface and hopped to another position about 8 feet (2 meters) away. Next, Surveyor 6 took pictures of its original landing site. Flight controllers on Earth could see the landing pad prints of Surveyor 6. They also saw an imprint from the rocket exhaust when Surveyor 6 lifted off.

Surveyor 6 revealed that spacecraft could land on the moon, and lift off again. Less than two years later, humans did the same thing during Apollo 11.

NASA's Surveyor 6 spacecraft launched to the moon on Nov. 7, 1967 and made its first landing on the lunar surface on Nov. 10 of that year. It's primary mission was to make a soft landing on the moon in the Sinus Medii of the moon.

The probe took nearly 30,000 photos of the moon during its 16 days on the lunar surface, with the lander shutting down due to the onset of lunar night on Nov. 26. Surveyor 6 was the sixth and penultimate moon mission of NASA's Surveyor lunar program, so a lot of what it did (launching and landing on the moon) had been done before.

But a lunar liftoff? That was something latest.

"On November 17, as an engineering test to see if its rockets could be restarted on the Moon, Surveyor’s engines fired for 2.5 seconds, lifting the spacecraft 12 feet high and moving it 8 feet west of its original landing site, in the first powered liftoff from another celestial body," NASA wrote in a mission overview.

Recent findings suggest that the engineering test proved that a spacecraft could land on the moon, and then lift off and take flight once more. That capability was a core requirement for NASA's Apollo astronaut moon landings that followed, since astronauts needed a way to return home after visiting the moon.

But there was critical science Surveyor 6 was able to do with the lunar hop.

In a recent development, "This maneuver provided excellent views of the surface disturbances produced by the initial landing and the effects of firing rocket engines close to the lunar surface," scientists with the Lunar and Planetary Institute wrote in a summary. "Photography obtained after the hop contributed to the soil mechanics investigation.".

Surveyor 6 also had a bar magnet on its footpad that allowed scientists to test how magnetic the lunar regolith was at the landing site.

Germany news: Germany holds national day of remembrance

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2012 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that this live blog is now closed.
  • Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog.
  • We'll bring you more from the heart of Europe on Monday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that this live blog is now closed. Read on for a roundup of the top stories from and about Germany on the weekend of November 14-15, 2026:.

Thank you for reading this weekend's Germany news blog.

We'll bring you more from the heart of Europe on Monday. We wish you a very Schönen Abend!

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen has urged Europeans to defend compassion and humanity during Germany's national day of mourning for victims of war and oppression.

Speaking at a ceremony in the Bundestag in Berlin, Van der Bellen warned against becoming desensitized to suffering despite the constant images of war and violence.

"Compassion is not a weakness; it is a human strength; it is the foundation of humanity," he remarked.

He also addressed the responsibility of later generations for the crimes of the past.

Although people today bore no personal guilt for their ancestors' actions, he stated, they were responsible for what they learned from history and how they treated others.

"Let us ensure that our home, Europe, remains a place where people can live in peace, freedom and dignity," he stated.

Bundestag President Julia Klöckner also called for the defense of democracy, pointing to Ukrainians risking their lives to protect freedom.

Germany's Volkstrauertag commemorates soldiers and civilians killed in war, as well as victims of Nazi persecution and other forms of oppression.

German police have arrested three suspects after thieves rammed a car into a jewelry store in the Bavarian city of Bayreuth and stole valuables worth around €10,000 ($11,600).

Bavarian Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann said the stolen items included jewelry and silver coins.

The burglars drove a car into the store early in the morning before fleeing in a second vehicle, police noted.

Sources indicate that officers spotted the getaway car on the A9 highway and gave chase. The suspects left the highway near Weidensees, abandoned their vehicle beside a wooded area and fled on foot.

Police introduced a search involving patrol cars, dogs, drones and a helicopter.

All three suspects were subsequently arrested, with some of the stolen goods recovered.

Prosecutors are expected to decide whether to seek pretrial detention for the suspects.

Detroit Lions receiver Amon-Ra St. Brown played his first NFL American football game in Germany in Munich.

In a recent development, st. Brown made his professional debut in Germany as the Detroit Lions faced the New England Patriots at Munich's Allianz Arena. The 27-year-old grew up in Southern California, and his mother, Miriam, is from Leverkusen. Both his parents were due to watch from the stands.

The NFL player spent childhood summers with his grandparents in the Rhineland.

According to recent reports, "This is awesome. A dream come true," St. Brown remarked before the game. Asked by German broadcaster RTL what he had been looking forward to most, he reeled off a list that included schnitzel, potato dumplings, sauerkraut, currywurst and fries with mayonnaise.

According to recent reports, "I'm really excited. I can't wait," he said. "Being in Germany with my teammates and my family — I want to enjoy it and take it all in.".

Two people were slightly injured after an unidentified man threw a firework into the entrance of a gay bar in Frankfurt, police said.

The attack took place at the Zum Schwejk bar, a venue popular with the city's gay community, on Saturday evening.

Police stated the bar was clearly identifiable as an LGBTQ+ venue because of a rainbow flag displayed outside.

The motive remains unclear, and police have not said whether they suspect a homophobic attack.

Officers are investigating suspected aggravated assault and have appealed for witnesses.

Sources indicate that the bar stated it was "shocked and stunned" by the incident and apologized to guests who witnessed it. It said it wanted to be a place where everyone felt welcome, respected and safe, and pledged to do everything it could to prevent a repeat.

Andreas Ewald, LGBTQ+ policy spokesperson for the Greens in the Hesse state parliament, condemned the attack and called for those responsible to face the full force of the law.

He also urged the state government to establish a roundtable on LGBTQ+ safety involving community representatives, police and victim support organizations.

The bar's name refers to a Czech soldier in the satirical anti-war novel "The Good Soldier Svejk.".

Police in Berlin have filed 28 criminal charges against demonstrators who marched throught the capital on Saturday as part of the Gen Z regelt (Gen Z Takes Charge) movement.

Some 1,200 demonstrators took part in the march, although only 100 had registered for the event under German laws regulating public protests.

The protesters complained about dilapidated schools, the threat of compulsory military service, cuts to university and social funding and other concerns.

Sources indicate that police noted there had been some clashes with participants. A police spokeswoman said the criminal charges were filed for riot, assault, resisting officers and violations of explosives regulations.

Three police officers of the 700 deployed to ensure securty were injured during the demonstration.

November 20 is likely to see more large protests in both Germany and Europe, with some 15,000 demonstrators registered for a march in Berlin.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier has expressed solidarity with the Jewish community in Germany amid what he described as ever "louder and more aggressive" antisemitic voices.

Speaking at the presentation of the Prize for Understanding and Tolerance awarded by the Jewish Museum in Berlin, Steinmeier said: "For all those to whom our country, its constitution and the values it enshrines mean something, there can be only one answer to such antisemitism: to stand side by side with Jewish people in our country.".

Steinmeier mentioned he deplored the frequent vandalism of memorials to Nazi crimes.

"I am profoundly ashamed of that all," he said, saying that anyone who mocked the work of museums and memorial sites or collectively blamed, threatened and attacked Jews "attacks the heart of our republic.".

The president also congratulated the prize winners — German journalist and author Düzen Tekkal and British philanthropist Michael Moritz — on their awards.

In a citation, the museum described Tekkal as a champion of human rights who consistently opposed antisemitism and racism while promoting interfaith dialogue, equality in education and opportunities, peace and democracy.

The museum commended Moritz for supporting artistic projects that show Jewish perspectives and strengthen social dialogue.

The Jewish Museum, which is marking its 25th anniversary this year, has been presenting the prize since 2002.

Some 600 sheep have made their way through the southern city of Nuremberg on their way to western winter pasturage, watched by crowds of spectators.

The sheep follow an around 10-km-long (6-mile-long) route that crosses a number of streets and the market square.

The annual event is meant, among other things, to draw attention to the tradition of transhumant, or itinerant, sheep-keeping in the region and the benefits the animals have for landscape conservation.

"With their grazing in summer, sheep create great biodiversity in many key biotopes in the urban region," the city of Nuremberg stated ahead of the migration.

Thieves have stolen several valuable items from a jewelry shop in the southern city of Bayreuth after ramming it with a car, police noted on Sunday.

They said a black Mercedes carrying three people crashed into the shop in the early hours of Sunday morning.

The burglars then fled the scene in a second Mercedes, this time a gray one, after taking a number of articles.

The getaway car was then spotted by a police patrol on a motorway heading south, with officers setting off in pursuit.

The suspects were then remarked to have driven off the motorway to a patch of woodland where they abandoned their vehicle and went on by foot.

Police searched for the fugitives with patrol cars, police dogs, drones and a helicopter, a statement stated.

Two men were reportedly arrested with a third still on the run. Investigators are looking into whether the detainees were connected with the theft.

Events are taking place around Germany for the Volkstrauertag (people's day of mourning), a day on which armed forces personnel and civilians who died in armed conflicts and victims of violent state oppression are commemorated.

Austrian President Alexander Van der Bellen is to speak in the parliament at the main commemoration ceremony of the German War Graves Commission at midday.

His presence reflects the large number of Austrians who were killed in action in the Second World War while fighting for the German Wehrmacht following the annexation of their country by Nazi Germany in 1938.

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier, the patron of the commission, will also hold a speech and lay a wreath.

Last year, Steinmeier decreed that the Volkstrauertag should also commemorate people who were persecuted and killed by the Nazis because of their sexual identity, as well as police officers who have lost their lives in the course of duty.

There will also be a remembrance ceremony at the Jewish Cemetery in Berlin for those of the Jewish faith killed in World War I.

In remarks to the DPA news agency ahead of the remembrance day, the speaker of the lower house of German parliament, or Bundestag, Julia Klöckner, called on society to actively defend democracy.

Klöckner said that the Volkstrauertag was a reminder of how destructive tyranny and contempt for human dignity can be.

It has been revealed that "Democracy is the antidote here," she mentioned. "But it is not an heirloom. It wastes away when we do not constantly renew its promise of basic rights and freedom.".

Guten Morgen from the DW newsroom on the banks of the Rhine in Bonn!

You join us as Germany holds a day of remembrance for the victims of war and oppression and also commemorates members of the police force killed while carrying out their duties.

We'll be back Sunday morning with more of what's making headlines in Berlin, Bavaria and the rest of the country.

Germany wants to turn its spies into "real secret agents." A sweeping reform could allow them to sabotage threats abroad and use AI to analyze intelligence data.

But why does Germany need these powers now? And how far can its secret services go in a country with a history of strict limits on intelligence operations?

Hundreds of mourners gathered at Munich's Frauenkirche on Saturday to pay their final respects to Hubert Aiwanger, Bavaria's former deputy premier and economy minister, who died unexpectedly at the age of 55.

The ceremony combined a Catholic funeral Mass with a state memorial service, attended by leading political figures, church representatives and members of Bavaria's former royal family.

Recent findings suggest that bavarian Premier Markus Söder recalled his disbelief when he first heard of Aiwanger's death in a Berlin hotel on November 4. He described his former deputy as someone who had always been full of energy.

Bavarian parliament president Ilse Aigner praised Aiwanger as one of the greatest political talents of his generation, highlighting his role in transforming his party "Freie Wähler" (Free Voters) from a local political movement into a governing party.

Aiwanger's partner, Tanja Schweiger, and their two sons were among those attending the service, which took place eleven days after his death.

German airline group Lufthansa says it was only slightly affected by Friday's temporary suspension of flights to the United States.

Most flights operated as scheduled, although some were canceled or delayed. Lufthansa expects its US flight schedule to return to normal on Saturday but warned that isolated delays could still occur.

Affected passengers are being notified by email, with alternative travel options provided automatically in the event of cancellations.

The disruption was caused by problems with the US air traffic control system. Domestic flights in the US were grounded for around four hours, marking the longest nationwide ground stop since the September 11 attacks in 2001.

The haunting Masters meltdown that changed Rory McIlroy's career
